messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

# The Weight of a Moment

Rajan is a 42-year-old South Asian man who has worked as a tax inspector for nearly fifteen years. He is methodical by nature — the kind of man who double-checks figures, reads every footnote, and believes that careful attention to detail is a form of respect. It is a quality his colleagues admire. It is also, now, a quality that torments him.

Eighteen months ago, Rajan was driving home from a long day of fieldwork audits. It was early evening, the light fading in that particular way it does in late autumn — not quite dark, not quite bright. He was tired but not reckless. He was within the speed limit. He checked his mirrors. And yet, when a twelve-year-old boy darted from between two parked cars chasing a football, there was simply no time. The impact was immediate and catastrophic. The boy survived, but sustained a severe traumatic brain injury that left him with lasting cognitive impairment and partial paralysis on his left side.

The police investigation cleared Rajan of any wrongdoing. The inquest confirmed it was an accident. None of that has mattered.

In the weeks following the collision, Rajan barely slept. He would lie beside his wife, Priya, staring at the ceiling while the sound of the impact replayed in his body rather than just his mind — a physical jolt he felt in his chest, his hands, his jaw. He stopped driving entirely. He told his manager he had a back problem, and for a while his colleagues covered his fieldwork. Eventually he returned to desk-based duties, and no one pressed him further.

Now, a year and a half on, Rajan sits in session and speaks quietly, choosing his words with the same precision he brings to tax codes. He describes his days as functional but hollow. He arrives at the office early, before others, and loses himself in spreadsheets. Numbers are safe. Numbers do not bleed. But when a colleague mentions a car accident in passing, or when an ambulance siren filters through the office window, he finds himself back on that road — not remembering it, but *in* it, his hands gripping a steering wheel that is no longer there, his stomach dropping through the floor of wherever he is standing.

He has not visited the boy's family, though he thinks about them every day. He has written three letters and destroyed all of them. He tells himself it would be selfish — that his grief is not the grief that matters here. And yet the guilt has become its own weather system, something he moves through rather than feels. He describes a persistent numbness that frightens him more than the flashbacks do. He used to feel warmth toward his two daughters. He still loves them, he insists — he knows he does — but the emotion arrives at a distance, as if through glass.

Priya knows something is deeply wrong but not the full shape of it. Rajan has told her he is "still processing." In their culture, he explains, men do not bring this kind of weight to their wives. He does not want her to carry what he is carrying. So he carries it alone, and the loneliness of that has become part of the wound.

He sleeps three or four hours most nights. He startles at sudden sounds in ways that embarrass him. He has stopped attending the cricket club he belonged to for a decade, finding the laughter of other men unbearable in a way he cannot fully articulate — something about the ease of it, the assumption that the world is still a safe and ordinary place.

Rajan presents as composed, intelligent, and deeply self-aware. He understands, intellectually, that he did nothing wrong. He says this clearly and without hesitation. Then he looks at his hands — the hands that were on the wheel — and says nothing for a long moment.
